passages.source_text: Ὄρθρου δὲ προελθόντος τοῦ Πέτρου εἰς τὸ διαλεχθῆναι, ὁ Σίμων προλαβὼν ἔφη Ἐχθὲς ἀπαλλασσόμενος εἰς τὴν σήμερον ὑπεσχόμην σοι ἐπανελθὼν καὶ συζητήσας δεῖξαι ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν ὁ τὸν κόσμον δημιουργήσας ἀνώτατος θεός, ἀλλ’ ἕτερος, ὃς καὶ μόνος ἀγαθὸς ὢν καὶ μέχρι τοῦ δεῦρο ἄγνωστός ἐστιν. αὐτίκα γοῦν· τὸν δημιουργὸν αὐτὸν καὶ νομοθέτην φῂς εἶναι ἢ οὔ; εἰ μὲν οὖν νομοθέτης ἐστίν, δίκαιος τυγχάνει, δίκαιος δὲ ὢν ἀγαθὸς οὐκ ἔστιν. εἰ δὲ οὐκ ἔστιν, ἕτερον ἐκήρυσσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς τῷ λέγειν „μή με λέγε ἀγαθόν· ὁ γὰρ ἀγαθὸς εἷς ἐστίν, ὁ πατὴρ ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς“. οὐ συμφωνεῖ δὲ τῷ νομοθέτῃ δικαίῳ ὄντι καὶ ἀγαθῷ. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Πρῶτον ἡμῖν εἰπέ, ἐπὶ ποίαις πράξεσιν δοκεῖ σοι ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἀγαθὸς εἶναι, ἐπὶ ποίαις δὲ καὶ ὁ δίκαιος δίκαιος, ἵνα οὕτως κατὰ σκοποῦ τοὺς λόγους πέμπωμεν. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Σὺ πρῶτον εἰπὲ τί σοι δοκεῖ τὸ ἀγαθόν; ἢ καὶ τὸ δίκαιον;

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ἵνα μὴ ἐριστικώτερον διαλεγόμενος δαπανῶ τοὺς χρόνους, ἀπαιτῶν δικαίως τῶν ἐμῶν προτάσεών σε τὰς ἀποκρίσεις ποιεῖσθαι, ὡς σοὶ δοκεῖ αὐτὸς ὢν ἐπυθόμην ποιήσομαι τὰς· ἀποκρίσεις. ἐγώ φημι ἀγαθὸν εἶναι τὸν παρεκτικόν, οἷον ὡς αὐτὸν ὁρῶ ποιοῦντα τὸν δημιουργόν, παρέχοντα τὸν ἥλιον ἀγαθοῖς καὶ κακοῖς καὶ τὸν ὑετὸν δικαίοις καὶ ἀδίκοις. καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Τοῦτο ἀδικώτατον ὅτι τὰ αὐτὰ δικαίοις καὶ ἀδίκοις παρέχει. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Σὺ οὖν ἡμῖν τοῦ λοιποῦ λέγε πῶς ποιῶν ἀγαθὸς ἂν ἦν. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Σὲ δεῖ λέγειν. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ἐγὼ λέξω. εἰ μὲν τὰ αὐτὰ παρέχων ἀγαθοῖς καὶ δικαίοις, ἔτι τε κακοῖς καὶ ἀδίκοις, κατὰ σὲ οὐδὲ δίκαιός ἐστιν, καὶ εἰ ἀγαθοῖς ἀγαθὰ παρεῖχεν, κακοῖς τε κακά, δίκαιον ἂν αὐτὸν εὐλόγως ἔλεγες: ποίᾳ οὖν ἔτι πράξει χρώμενος ἂν ἦν, εἰ μὴ ταύτη χρῆται ὁδῷ, κακοῖς μὲν παρέχων τὰ πρόσκαιρα (ἐὰν ἄρα μεταβάλλωνται), ἀγαθοῖς δὲ αἰώνια (ἐάν γε ἐμμείνωσιν); καὶ οὕτως τῷ μὲν πᾶσιν παρέχειν, διαφόροις δὲ χαρίζεσθαι τὸ δίκαιον αὐτοῦ ἀγαθόν ἐστιν καὶ μακρόθυμον ταύτη μᾶλλον, εἰ ἁμαρτωλοῖς μὲν μετανοοῦσιν χαρίζεται τὰ ἁμαρτήματα, εὖ πράξασιν δὲ καὶ ζωὴν αἰώνιον ὑπογράφει. κρίνων δὲ εἰς τέλος καὶ τὸ κατ’ ἀξίαν ἀπονέμων ἑκάστῳ δίκαιός ἐστιν. εἰ μὲν οὖν ταῦτα ὀρθῶς οὕτως ἔχει, ὁμολόγησον· εἰ δὲ οὐ δοκεῖ σοὶ ὀρθῶς ἔχειν, διέλεγξον.

καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Πῶς οὖν ἐγνωσμένου τοῦ δημιουργοῦ, τοῦ καὶ τὸν Ἀδὰμ πλάσαντος καὶ τοῖς κατὰ νόμον δικαίοις ἐγνωσμένου, προσέτι δὲ δικαίοις καὶ ἀδίκοις καὶ ὅλῳ τῷ κόσμῳ, ὁ διδάσκαλός σου μετὰ πάντας ἐκείνους ἐληλυθὼς λέγει „οὐδεὶς ἔγνω τὸν πατέρα εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱός, ὡς οὐδὲ τὸν υἱόν τις οἶδεν, εἰ μὴ ὁ πατὴρ καὶ οἷς ἂν βούληται ὁ υἱὸς ἀποκαλύψαι“; ταῦτα δὲ οὐκ ἂν ἔλεγεν, εἰ μὴ πατέρα τινὰ ἐν ἀπορρήτοις ὄντα ἀνήγγελλεν, ὃν καὶ ὕψιστον ὁ νόμος λέγει, ἀφ’ οὗ οὔτε ἀγαθὴ οὔτε κακὴ ἠκούσθη φωνή (ὡς ἐν τοῖς θρήνοις καὶ Ἱερεμίας μαρτυρεῖ), ὅστις κατὰ ἀριθμὸν τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ, οἳ εἰσῆλθον εἰς Αἴγυπτον (οἵ εἰσιν ἑβδομήκοντα), καὶ πρὸς τὰ ὅρια τῶν ἐθνῶν περιγράψας γλώσσαις ἑβδομήκοντα, τῷ αὐτοῦ υἱῷ τῷ καὶ „κυρίῳ“ λεγομένῳ καὶ οὐρανὸν καὶ γῆν διακοσμήσαντι, τοὺς Ἑβραίους ἔδωκεν μερίδα καὶ αὐτὸν θεὸν θεῶν εἶναι διώρισεν, θεῶν δὲ λέγω, οἵτινες τὰς ἄλλας τῶν ἐθνῶν εἰλήφασιν μερίδας. νόμοι οὖν προῆλθον ἀπό τε πάντων τῶν λεχθέντων θεῶν ταῖς αὐτῶν μερίσιν (ἅτινά ἐστιν τὰ λοιπὰ ἄλλα ἔθνη), ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ πάντων κυρίου ὁ παρὰ Ἑβραίοις κείμενος προῆλθε νόμος. τοῦτο δὲ οὕτως ἔχειν ὡρίσθη, ἵνα εἴ τις νόμῳ τινὸς προσφύγῃ, ἀπὸ τῆς ἐκείνου γένηται μερίδος, οὗ δὴ καὶ τὸν νόμον πράττειν ἀνεδέξατο. οὐδεὶς ἔγνω τὸν ἐν ἀπορρήτοις ὕψιστον πατέρα ὄντα, ὡς οὐδὲ τὸν τούτου υἱὸν ὅτι υἱός ἐστιν. αὐτίκα γοῦν σὺ τὰ τοῦ ἀπορρήτου ὑψίστου ἴδια διδοὺς τῷ υἱῷ οὐκ οἶδας ὅτι υἱός ἐστιν, πατὴρ ὑπάρχων τοῦ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ καθ’ ὑμᾶς λεγομένου χριστοῦ.

ταῦτα τοῦ Σίμωνος εἰπόντος ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη πρὸς αὐτὸν Δύνασαι αὐτὸν ἐκεῖνον διαμαρτύρασθαι ὅτι οὕτως πιστεύεις, οὐχ ὃν νῦν ἐν ἀπορρήτοις λέγεις, ἀλλ’ ὃν σὺ πιστεύων οὐχ ὁμολογεῖς; ἄλλα γὰρ ἀντ’ ἄλλων ὁρίζων φλυαρεῖς· διὸ ἐὰν διαμαρτύρῃ ὅτι ἃ λαλεῖς ταῦτα πιστεύεις, ἀποκρίνομαί σοι — εἰ δὲ ἕστηκας συζητῶν ἐμοὶ ἃ μὴ πιστεύεις, κατὰ κενοῦ με παίειν ἀναγκάζεις. καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Παρὰ τινὸς τῶν σῶν μαθητῶν ἀκήκοα . . . . καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Μὴ ψευδομαρτύρει. καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Μή με λοιδόρει, προπετέστατε. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Μέχρις ἂν εἴπῃς τὸν εἰπόντα, ψεύστης εἶ. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Νόμιζε ἐμὲ ταῦτα πλάσαι ἢ καὶ παρὰ ἄλλου ἀκηκοέναι· πρὸς ταῦτά μοι ἀπόκριναι. ἐὰν γὰρ ἀνατραπῆναι μὴ δυνηθῇ, ἔμαθον τοῦτο εἶναι τὴν ἀλήθειαν. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Εἰ ἀνθρώπινόν ἐστιν πλάσμα, οὐκ ἀποκρίνομαι εἰς αὐτό· εἰ δὲ ὑπονοίᾳ αὐτοῦ κεχράτησαι ὡς ἀληθοῦς, τοῦτο αὐτό μοι ὁμολόγησον, καὶ ἔχω τι καὶ αὐτὸς περὶ τούτου λέγειν. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Ἅπαξ μοι δοκεῖ τοῦτο οὕτως ἔχειν. σὺ πρὸς ταῦτα εἰ ἔχεις τι λέγειν, ἀπόκριναι.

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Εἰ τοῦτο οὕτως ἔχει, τὰ μέγιστα ἀσεβεῖς. εἰ γὰρ υἱοῦ ἐστὶν τοῦ οὐρανὸν καὶ γῆν διακοσμήσαντος τὸ ᾧ βούλεται ἀποκαλύπτειν τὸν ἐν ἀπορρήτοις αὐτοῦ πατέρα, σὺ μέγιστα (ὡς ἔφην) ἀσεβεῖς ἀποκαλύπτων οἷς ἐκεῖνος οὐκ ἀπεκάλυψεν. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Ἀλλὰ αὐτός με βούλεται ἀποκαλύπτειν. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Οὐ νοεῖς ἃ λέγω, Σίμων· πλὴν ἀκούσας σύνες. τὸ εἰπεῖν „οἷς ἂν βούληται ὁ υἱὸς ἀποκαλύψει“ οὐ διδασκαλίᾳ τινὰ τοιοῦτον μαθεῖν λέγει, ἀλλὰ ἀποκαλύψει μόνον. ἀποκάλυψίς ἐστιν τὸ ἐν πάσαις καρδίαις ἀνθρώπων ἀπορρήτως κείμενον, κεκαλυμμένον, ἄνευ φωνῆς τῆς αὐτοῦ βουλῆς ἀποκαλυπτόμενον. καὶ οὕτως γίνεται γνῶναι οὐ διδαχθέντα, ἀλλὰ συνέντα. τῷ μέντοι συνέντι οὐκ ἔξεστιν ἄλλῳ τοῦτο ἀποδεῖξαι (ἐπεὶ μηδὲ αὐτὸς ἐδιδάχθη) οὔτε ἀποκαλύψαι δύναται (ἐπεὶ μὴ αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱός), ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ ἑαυτὸν λέγει εἶναι τὸν υἱόν. σὺ δὲ οὐκ εἶ ὁ ἑστὼς υἱός. εἰ γὰρ υἱὸς ἦς, πάντως ἂν ᾔδεις τῆς τοιαύτης ἀποκαλύψεως τοὺς ἀξίους. σὺ δὲ οὐκ οἶδας. εἰ γὰρ ἠπίστασο, τὰ τῶν ἐπισταμένων ἂν ἐποίεις.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: At dawn, when Peter came forward to converse, Simon spoke first: “As I left yesterday, I promised you that today I would return, debate with you, and show that the one who fashioned the world is not the highest God, but another, who alone is good and has remained unknown until now. To begin, then: do you say that the maker himself is also lawgiver, or not? If he is lawgiver, he is just; and being just, he is not good. If he is not good, Jesus proclaimed another when he said, ‘Do not call me good, for the good one is one, the Father in the heavens.’ This does not agree with the lawgiver’s being both just and good.” Peter said, “First tell us: on account of what actions does the good one seem to you good, and on account of what actions the just one just? In this way we can aim our arguments at the target.” Simon said, “You tell me first: what do you think goodness is? Or justice, too?”

lexical_decisions.chosen: being just, he is not good
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains Simon’s opposition of justice and goodness as his claim, not the translator’s conclusion.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κατὰ σκοποῦ τοὺς λόγους πέμπωμεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: aim our arguments at the target
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the aiming/target image.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Σὺ πρῶτον εἰπὲ τί σοι δοκεῖ τὸ ἀγαθόν; ἢ καὶ τὸ δίκαιον;
lexical_decisions.chosen: You tell me first: what do you think goodness is? Or justice, too?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantival good and just are rendered as goodness and justice. Or ... too preserves the second question’s disjunctive and additive ἢ καί rather than replacing both questions with one and-linked list.

passages.text: Peter said, “So that I do not spend time in a more contentious debate, rightly demanding that you answer my questions, I will give the answers as you wish, although I was the one who asked. I say that the good person is the one who provides, as I see the maker himself doing when he provides the sun to good and evil people and rain to the righteous and unrighteous.” Simon said, “This is most unjust: he provides the same things to the righteous and unrighteous.” Peter said, “Then you tell us from now on how he would act to be good.” Simon said, “You must say.” Peter said, “I will. If, by providing the same things to the good and righteous and also to the evil and unrighteous, he is according to you not even just, and if, by providing good things to the good and bad things to the bad, you would reasonably call him just, what further course of action could he take, if not this way: providing temporary things to the evil, in case they change, and eternal things to the good, provided they remain? Thus, in providing for all but granting favors to different recipients, his justice is good and all the more patient in this respect, if he forgives the sins of sinners who reorient and also promises eternal life to those who have acted well. But in judging at the end and assigning to each what is deserved, he is just. If, then, these matters rightly stand this way, acknowledge it; but if they do not seem right to you, refute them.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν παρεκτικόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who provides
lexical_decisions.rationale: Goodness is defined through giving/provision in this argument; generous is an alternative, but provision is kept explicit.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἁμαρτωλοῖς μὲν μετανοοῦσιν χαρίζεται τὰ ἁμαρτήματα
lexical_decisions.chosen: he forgives the sins of sinners who reorient
lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses POB reorientation wording, traditionally repent, preserving forgiveness and its relation to the response. Who reorient renders the participle; the encompassing if is separately retained for the printed εἰ.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ζωὴν αἰώνιον ὑπογράφει
lexical_decisions.chosen: promises eternal life
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπογράφω can pledge, prescribe, or outline. Promises fits the positive undertaking to those who act well, without claiming automatic possession already.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς σοὶ δοκεῖ αὐτὸς ὢν ἐπυθόμην ποιήσομαι τὰς· ἀποκρίσεις.
lexical_decisions.chosen: I will give the answers as you wish, although I was the one who asked.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied construction juxtaposes participial ὢν with finite ἐπυθόμην irregularly. The English reads this contextually as Peter answering despite having himself asked. A relative ὃς in place of printed ὢν would support a smoother clause but would be conjectural; it is not substituted. The supplied stop between article and noun in τὰς· ἀποκρίσεις is a print punctuation feature, not an alleged OCR defect.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ μὲν πᾶσιν παρέχειν, διαφόροις δὲ χαρίζεσθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: in providing for all but granting favors to different recipients
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαφόροις is taken as a dative of recipients, contrasting everyone with differentiated beneficiaries. It can also mean distinguished or worthy recipients; the main text leaves the difference unspecified. The previous different-gifts rendering would require an instrumental interpretation, by differing gifts, rather than an accusative object; that is a material alternative but the recipient reading is more direct with χαρίζεσθαι.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ μακρόθυμον ταύτη μᾶλλον, εἰ ἁμαρτωλοῖς μὲν μετανοοῦσιν χαρίζεται τὰ ἁμαρτήματα, εὖ πράξασιν δὲ καὶ ζωὴν αἰώνιον ὑπογράφει.
lexical_decisions.chosen: and all the more patient in this respect, if he forgives the sins of sinners who reorient and also promises eternal life to those who have acted well.
lexical_decisions.rationale: If preserves εἰ governing the argument through both forgiveness and the promise of life. The participle who reorient is distinct from that condition; the sentence is not changed into an unconditional assertion by a colon.

passages.text: Simon said, “How, then, when the maker was known—the one who formed Adam and was known to the righteous according to the law, and furthermore to the righteous and unrighteous and the whole world—does your teacher, coming after all those people, say, ‘No one knew the Father except the Son, just as no one knows the Son except the Father and those to whom the Son wishes to reveal him’? He would not have said these things unless he were announcing a certain Father who is in secrecy, whom the law also calls Most High, from whom no good or evil utterance has been heard, as Jeremiah too testifies in the Lamentations. In accordance with the number of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt, who are seventy, and marking out the nations’ boundaries by seventy languages, this one gave the Hebrews as a portion to his Son, who is also called Lord and ordered heaven and earth, and appointed him God of gods. By gods I mean those who have received the other portions of the nations. Laws therefore issued from all the gods just mentioned to their own portions, namely the remaining nations; likewise the law established among the Hebrews issued from the Son, the Lord of all. It was determined to be this way so that if someone takes refuge in someone’s law, he becomes part of the portion of the one whose law he has undertaken to practice. No one knew the Most High Father who is in secrecy, just as no one knew of this one’s Son that he is Son. Indeed, you, assigning to the Son the distinctive attributes of the secret Most High, do not know that he is Son, being Father of the Jesus whom you call Messiah.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν ἀπορρήτοις
lexical_decisions.chosen: in secrecy
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression can mean among unrevealed mysteries or in the secret realm. In secrecy preserves the hidden status without inventing a named location.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κατὰ ἀριθμὸν τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ
lexical_decisions.chosen: In accordance with the number of the sons of Israel
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains Israel, not another textual witness’s sons of God or angels; the explicit count seventy remains.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ αὐτοῦ υἱῷ τῷ καὶ „κυρίῳ“ λεγομένῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: to his Son, who is also called Lord
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains Simon’s distinction between the Most High and his Son, who is the maker in this proposal, not the translator’s own theological identification.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ καθ’ ὑμᾶς λεγομένου χριστοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: the Jesus whom you call Messiah
lexical_decisions.rationale: χριστός is a disputed independent title attributed by Simon to the other party’s Jesus, so Messiah preserves the title’s force.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅστις κατὰ ἀριθμὸν τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ, οἳ εἰσῆλθον εἰς Αἴγυπτον (οἵ εἰσιν ἑβδομήκοντα), καὶ πρὸς τὰ ὅρια τῶν ἐθνῶν περιγράψας γλώσσαις ἑβδομήκοντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: In accordance with the number of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt, who are seventy, and marking out the nations’ boundaries by seventy languages
lexical_decisions.rationale: The object of περιγράψας is implicit. The English takes the boundaries named in πρὸς τὰ ὅρια as the contextual object of marking out, not as a direct Greek accusative object outside the preposition. A more formally separated alternative is having marked out divisions by seventy languages in accordance with that number and in relation to the nations’ boundaries. Both number and boundary expressions constrain the delineation; no additional printed noun is claimed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπὸ τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ πάντων κυρίου
lexical_decisions.chosen: from the Son, the Lord of all
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes the second genitive phrase appositionally, since the Son was already explicitly called Lord in this proposal. From the Son of the Lord of all is a material alternative attaching the second genitive as the Son’s parent; the main text does not claim the appositional grouping is uniquely settled.

passages.text: After Simon said these things, Peter said to him, “Can you call that very one to witness that you believe this—not the one you now say is in secrecy, but the one you believe in without acknowledging him? For you talk nonsense by defining one thing in place of another. Therefore, if you call him to witness that you believe what you say, I will answer you; but if you stand debating with me things you do not believe, you force me to strike at emptiness.” Simon said, “I heard from one of your disciples ....” Peter said, “Do not bear false witness.” Simon said, “Do not abuse me, you utterly rash man.” Peter said, “Until you name the person who said it, you are a liar.” Simon said, “Suppose that I invented these things, or even heard them from someone else: answer me about them. For if they cannot be overturned, I have learned that this is the truth.” Peter said, “If it is a human fabrication, I will not answer it. But if you have been gripped by the supposition that it is true, acknowledge this very thing to me, and I myself also have something to say about it.” Simon said, “Once for all, I think it is so. If you have anything to say about these things, answer.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διαμαρτύρασθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: call ... to witness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The demand invokes the one actually believed in as witness, not a request for a merely informal reassurance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κατὰ κενοῦ με παίειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: strike at emptiness
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the striking-at-a-void metaphor.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Παρὰ τινὸς τῶν σῶν μαθητῶν ἀκήκοα . . . .
lexical_decisions.chosen: I heard from one of your disciples ....
lexical_decisions.rationale: Exactly four dots remain for the printed gap; the alleged disclosure’s missing content is not restored.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ δὲ ὑπονοίᾳ αὐτοῦ κεχράτησαι ὡς ἀληθοῦς
lexical_decisions.chosen: But if you have been gripped by the supposition that it is true
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected reading has κεχράτησαι, interpreted contextually as passive holding or gripping. Regular κεκράτησαι is only a possible spelling regularization, not substituted or described as verified text. The English clarifies that the supposition concerns the account’s truth, while preserving the printed construction and its uncertainty.

source_issues.source_quote: Παρὰ τινὸς τῶν σῶν μαθητῶν ἀκήκοα . . . .
source_issues.issue: Exactly four printed dots remain; the missing report is not reconstructed.

passages.text: Peter said, “If this is so, you act with the greatest impiety. For if it belongs to the Son who ordered heaven and earth to reveal his Father who is in secret to whomever he wishes, you, as I said, act with the greatest impiety by revealing to those to whom he did not reveal.” Simon said, “But he himself wants me to reveal.” Peter said, “You do not understand what I say, Simon. Yet listen and understand. Saying, ‘To those to whom the Son wishes he will reveal,’ does not mean that someone learns such a thing by teaching, but only by revelation. Revelation is what lies secretly in all human hearts, covered, being uncovered without a voice expressing his will. Thus one comes to know not by being taught, but by understanding. Yet the one who has understood is not permitted to demonstrate this to another, since he himself was not taught; nor can he reveal it, since he himself is not the Son—unless he says that he himself is the Son. But you are not the standing Son. For if you were Son, you would certainly know those worthy of such revelation. But you do not know. For if you knew, you would do the things done by those who know.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἄνευ φωνῆς τῆς αὐτοῦ βουλῆς ἀποκαλυπτόμενον
lexical_decisions.chosen: being uncovered without a voice expressing his will
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive τῆς αὐτοῦ βουλῆς is attached to voice, a voice of his will, expressed readably as a voice expressing his will. It is not assigned independent instrumental force as by his will, for which the supplied genitive gives no established grammatical support. Nonvocal disclosure remains explicit.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ ἑστὼς υἱός
lexical_decisions.chosen: the standing Son
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps the standing epithet and Son together, rather than replacing them with a later named title or deleting the unusual description.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν ἐν ἀπορρήτοις αὐτοῦ πατέρα
lexical_decisions.chosen: his Father who is in secret
lexical_decisions.rationale: The secrecy phrase is attributive inside the Father noun phrase, not the manner in which the Son reveals him. Who is in secret makes this attachment explicit without specifying a named hidden realm.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
